newsitem.title: USA: NationsBank seen winner despite stock drop.
newsitem.headline: NationsBank seen winner despite stock drop.

text.p: NationsBank Corp chairman and chief executive Hugh McColl has proven again that he is one of the gutsiest acquirers in banking by paying a steep price to acquire Boatmen's Bancshares Inc and extend his franchise into the U.S. heartland, analysts said.
Although several Wall Street analysts cut ratings on NationsBank as its stock price fell Friday, others said McColl was making a bold move to seize a unique opportunity.
A key issue in the deal is the use of the purchase method of accounting instead of the more familiar pooling method.

"I think it's absolutely fabulous," said Robert Bonelli, executive vice president of Ernst & Co and president of Ernst Asset Management. "If you have to pay up for an organization like Boatmen's, which happens to be one of the best-run banks in the country, you pay up for it. You don't get the opportunity every day."

NationsBank told analysts its earnings per share pro forma are expected to be $8.48 per share in 1997. Analysts had been looking for earnings of $8.98 per share. With the transaction expected to close in January 1997, that would "dilute" earnings by about 5.6 percent in the first year.

According to an analyst who heard the presentation, NationsBank also said pro forma earnings would rise to about $10.00 per share in 1998 and then to $11.27 per share in 1999. NationsBank said that represented a slight "add" to 1998 earnings and a more meaningful boost in 1999, when forecast earnings for NationsBank as a stand-alone would have been $11.06 per share.
A key element is that the earnings projections are affected by the purchase accounting, rarely used in big bank deals until Wells Fargo & Co used it earlier this year to buy First Interstate Bancorp.
